options: The overall mean of the data, computed in advance
The smallest class mark in the distribution
Any convenient class mark, typically one near the middle of the distribution
The class mark of the class with the highest frequency, always
questions.explanation: The assumed mean is simply a convenient reference point (usually a middling class mark, to keep the step-deviations small)  -  the final variance turns out the same regardless of which class mark is chosen.
questions.hint: Think about why it's called an 'assumed' mean, and what makes a class mark convenient to work with.
distractor_logic: Computing the true mean first would defeat the purpose of the shortcut method, which is designed to avoid that calculation.
There is no requirement to choose the smallest class mark; any convenient class mark works equally well.
While the modal class mark is often a convenient choice, it is not mandatory  -  any class mark works, since the final result does not depend on this choice.

questions.topic: Variance and Standard Deviation — Continuous Data and the Shortcut Method
questions.question: In the step-deviation method, which substitution correctly defines \( u_i \) in terms of the class mark \( x_i \), the assumed mean \( A \), and the class width \( h \)?
options: \( u_i = \dfrac{x_i-A}{h} \)
\( u_i = \dfrac{x_i}{A-h} \)
\( u_i = x_i-A\times h \)
\( u_i = \dfrac{A-x_i}{h} \)
questions.explanation: The defining substitution is \( u_i=(x_i-A)/h \): subtract the assumed mean from the class mark, then divide by the class width.
questions.hint: Recall the exact order: subtract the assumed mean from the class mark first, then divide by the class width.
distractor_logic: This places the deviation in the denominator and mixes up \( A \) and \( h \) in a way that does not match the defining substitution.
This multiplies rather than divides by \( h \), and omits the division needed to standardise the deviation.
This reverses the sign of the deviation in the numerator  -  the correct formula subtracts \( A \) from \( x_i \), not the other way round.

questions.topic: Variance and Standard Deviation — Continuous Data and the Shortcut Method
questions.question: Which of the following is the correct step-deviation formula for the variance of a continuous frequency distribution?
options: \( \sigma^{2} = h\left[\dfrac{1}{N}\displaystyle\sum f_iu_i^{2} - \left(\dfrac{1}{N}\displaystyle\sum f_iu_i\right)^{2}\right] \)
\( \sigma^{2} = h^{2}\cdot\dfrac{1}{N}\displaystyle\sum f_iu_i^{2} \)
\( \sigma^{2} = h^{2}\left[\dfrac{1}{N}\displaystyle\sum f_iu_i^{2} - \left(\dfrac{1}{N}\displaystyle\sum f_iu_i\right)^{2}\right] \)
\( \sigma^{2} = h^{2}\left[\dfrac{1}{N}\displaystyle\sum f_iu_i^{2} + \left(\dfrac{1}{N}\displaystyle\sum f_iu_i\right)^{2}\right] \)
questions.explanation: The correct formula scales the bracketed step-deviation quantity back up by \( h^{2} \) and SUBTRACTS the squared mean of the step-deviations as a correction term: \( \sigma^{2}=h^{2}[\frac{1}{N}\sum f_iu_i^{2}-(\frac{1}{N}\sum f_iu_i)^{2}] \).
questions.hint: Two things to check: the final multiplier is \( h^{2} \) (not \( h \)), and the correction term is SUBTRACTED (not added).
distractor_logic: This multiplies by \( h \) instead of \( h^{2} \), forgetting that the step-deviation itself was scaled down by \( h \), so the correction needs to be scaled back up by \( h \) squared.
This drops the squared correction term entirely, which is needed whenever the mean of the step-deviations is not exactly zero.
This adds the squared correction term instead of subtracting it, which would overstate the variance.

questions.topic: Variance and Standard Deviation — Continuous Data and the Shortcut Method
questions.question: The ages (in years) of members registered at a community library are grouped as: class 0-10 has frequency 5; class 10-20 has frequency 8; class 20-30 has frequency 15; class 30-40 has frequency 16; class 40-50 has frequency 6. Using the step-deviation method with assumed mean \( A=25 \) and class width \( h=10 \), find the variance of this distribution.
questions.explanation: \( N=50 \). Using \( u_i = \dfrac{x_i-A}{h} \): \( u_1=\dfrac{5-25}{10}=-2, u_2=\dfrac{15-25}{10}=-1, u_3=\dfrac{25-25}{10}=0, u_4=\dfrac{35-25}{10}=1, u_5=\dfrac{45-25}{10}=2 \). Then \( f_1u_1=5\times(-2)=-10, f_2u_2=8\times(-1)=-8, f_3u_3=15\times0=0, f_4u_4=16\times1=16, f_5u_5=6\times2=12 \), giving \( \sum f_iu_i=10 \); and \( f_1u_1^{2}=5\times(-2)^{2}=20, f_2u_2^{2}=8\times(-1)^{2}=8, f_3u_3^{2}=15\times0^{2}=0, f_4u_4^{2}=16\times1^{2}=16, f_5u_5^{2}=6\times2^{2}=24 \), giving \( \sum f_iu_i^{2}=68 \). By \( \sigma^{2} = h^{2}\left[\dfrac{1}{N}\displaystyle\sum f_iu_i^{2} - \left(\dfrac{1}{N}\displaystyle\sum f_iu_i\right)^{2}\right] \), \( \sigma^{2}=10^{2}\left[\dfrac{68}{50}-\left(\dfrac{10}{50}\right)^{2}\right]=132 \). Checking by the direct method on the class marks gives \( \sigma^{2}=132 \) as well, confirming the shortcut.
questions.hint: Compute \( u_i=(x_i-A)/h \) for each class mark, then apply \( \sigma^{2}=h^{2}[\frac{1}{N}\sum f_iu_i^{2}-(\frac{1}{N}\sum f_iu_i)^{2}] \)  -  remember the final \( h^{2} \) multiplier.
distractor_logic: Comes from computing \( \frac{1}{N}\sum f_iu_i^{2}-(\frac{1}{N}\sum f_iu_i)^{2} \) correctly but forgetting to multiply back by \( h^{2} \).
Comes from computing \( h^{2}\times\frac{1}{N}\sum f_iu_i^{2} \) but forgetting to subtract the squared correction term \( h^{2}(\frac{1}{N}\sum f_iu_i)^{2} \).
Comes from taking the square root at the end  -  that gives the standard deviation, not the variance.

Using the step-deviation method with assumed mean \( A=35 \) and class width \( h=10 \), find the standard deviation of this distribution.

questions.question: The time (in seconds) taken by runners to finish a 100 m trial is grouped as: class 0-10 has frequency 6; class 10-20 has frequency 9; class 20-30 has frequency 13; class 30-40 has frequency 8; class 40-50 has frequency 4. Taking the class mark of each class as \( x_i \), find the standard deviation of this distribution using the direct method.
questions.explanation: \( N=40 \). Class marks give mean \( \bar{x}=23.75 \). Frequency-weighted squared deviations: \( f_i(x_i-\bar{x})^{2}=6\times(-18.75)^{2}=2109.375, f_i(x_i-\bar{x})^{2}=9\times(-8.75)^{2}=689.0625, f_i(x_i-\bar{x})^{2}=13\times1.25^{2}=20.3125, f_i(x_i-\bar{x})^{2}=8\times11.25^{2}=1012.5, f_i(x_i-\bar{x})^{2}=4\times21.25^{2}=1806.25 \). Sum \( \sum f_i(x_i-\bar{x})^{2}=5637.5 \). Using \( \sigma^{2} = \dfrac{1}{N}\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}f_i(x_i-\bar{x})^{2} \), \( \sigma^{2}=\dfrac{5637.5}{40}=140.9375 \). Standard deviation \( \sigma=\sqrt{\sigma^{2}}=\sqrt{140.9375}\approx11.872 \).
questions.hint: Replace each class by its mid-point first, then apply the direct-method variance formula exactly as for a discrete frequency table.
distractor_logic: Comes from averaging the squared deviations of the class marks over the number of classes instead of weighting each by its frequency.
Comes from reporting the variance itself and forgetting to take the square root.
Comes from taking the square root of \( \sum f_i(x_i-\bar{x})^{2} \) directly, without dividing by \( N \) first.

questions.topic: Variance and Standard Deviation — Continuous Data and the Shortcut Method
questions.question: Once the variance \( \sigma^{2} \) of a distribution has been computed by the step-deviation method, does the numerical result depend on which class mark was chosen as the assumed mean \( A \)?
options: No  -  any valid choice of \( A \) gives exactly the same final variance
Yes  -  choosing a larger \( A \) always gives a larger variance
Yes  -  choosing a smaller \( A \) always gives a larger variance
It depends on whether \( A \) is chosen as an even or an odd number
questions.explanation: The step-deviation formula's correction term exactly cancels out any dependence on the choice of assumed mean, so the final variance is the same no matter which class mark is used as \( A \)  -  that is precisely what makes it a valid shortcut.
questions.hint: Think about the role the correction term plays in removing the effect of an arbitrarily chosen reference point.
distractor_logic: The final formula correctly cancels out the choice of \( A \) through the correction term; a larger \( A \) does not systematically inflate the variance.
By the same reasoning, a smaller \( A \) does not systematically inflate the variance either  -  the correction term is designed precisely to remove this dependence.
Whether \( A \) is even or odd has no mathematical bearing on the formula  -  this is not a real factor in the computation at all.

questions.topic: Variance and Standard Deviation — Continuous Data and the Shortcut Method
questions.question: Why must all the class intervals have the same (equal) width \( h \) for the basic step-deviation method to be applied directly?
options: So that a single, common \( h \) can be used to convert every class mark into a simple integer step-deviation \( u_i \)
Because unequal class widths would make the total frequency \( N \) incorrect
Because the mean of the distribution cannot be computed unless the widths are equal
Because unequal class widths would make the frequencies negative
questions.explanation: The formula \( u_i=(x_i-A)/h \) uses one single value of \( h \) for every class; if the widths differed, each class would need its own divisor, and the simplified integer step-deviations  -  and the neat final formula  -  would no longer apply directly.
questions.hint: Think about what breaks if you try to use one shared divisor \( h \) for classes of different widths.
distractor_logic: The total frequency \( N \) is just the sum of the individual class frequencies and is unaffected by whether the class widths are equal or not.
The mean of a grouped distribution can be computed perfectly well even when class widths differ  -  unequal widths only complicate the shortcut substitution, not the mean itself.
Class widths, whether equal or unequal, are always positive quantities; unequal widths have no tendency to produce negative frequencies.

questions.topic: Variance and Standard Deviation — Continuous Data and the Shortcut Method
questions.question: In the step-deviation formula \( \sigma^{2}=h^{2}\left[\frac{1}{N}\sum f_iu_i^{2}-\left(\frac{1}{N}\sum f_iu_i\right)^{2}\right] \), why is the final multiplication by \( h^{2} \) necessary?
options: Because \( h \) is always an even number, and even numbers must be squared in every statistics formula
Because \( u_i \) was obtained by dividing the original deviation by \( h \), so the bracketed quantity is in squared-\( u \) units and must be scaled back to squared-\( x \) units
Because it corrects for the frequencies \( f_i \) not summing exactly to \( N \)
Because it converts the variance into the same units as the mean deviation
questions.explanation: Since \( u_i=(x_i-A)/h \), working entirely in \( u \) units shrinks every squared deviation by a factor of \( h^{2} \); multiplying the bracketed quantity back by \( h^{2} \) restores the variance to the original units of \( x \).
questions.hint: Trace what happens to the units of a squared deviation once every \( x_i \) has been divided by \( h \) to form \( u_i \).
distractor_logic: There is no rule linking squaring to \( h \) being even  -  this is not a real mathematical reason connected to the formula.
The frequencies summing to \( N \) is simply how \( N \) is defined; it has nothing to do with why a final \( h^{2} \) factor appears.
Variance and mean deviation are different measures with different formulas altogether; the \( h^{2} \) factor here has nothing to do with matching mean-deviation units.

topics.name: Range and Mean Deviation about the Mean
topics.summary: Dispersion measures how spread out a data set is around its centre. The simplest such measure is the range: the difference between the largest and the smallest observation, \( \text{Range} = x_{max} - x_{min} \). Range is easy to compute but only looks at the two extreme values, ignoring everything in between, so it can be misleading when a data set has outliers or is unevenly spread. The mean deviation about the mean improves on this by using every observation: it averages the absolute distance of each value from the mean, \( \text{M.D.}(\bar{x}) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}|x_i-\bar{x}| \) for individual data, or \( \text{M.D.}(\bar{x}) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{n}f_i|x_i-\bar{x}| \) for frequency data. The absolute value is essential: the signed deviations \( x_i-\bar{x} \) always sum to exactly zero, so without absolute values the measure would be meaningless. A larger mean deviation signals a more spread-out data set; a smaller one signals values clustered tightly around the mean.
topics.worked_example: For the data \( 4, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12, 13, 17 \): mean \( \bar{x}=10 \). Deviations \( x_i-\bar{x} \): \( -6,-3,-2,-1,0,2,3,7 \). Absolute deviations: \( 6,3,2,1,0,2,3,7 \), summing to \( 24 \). So \( \text{M.D.}(\bar{x})=\dfrac{24}{8}=3 \). The range of the same data is \( 17-4=13 \).
common_mistakes: Forgetting the absolute value and letting positive and negative deviations cancel to zero
Squaring the deviations instead of taking their absolute value (confusing mean deviation with variance)
Forgetting to weight by frequency \( f_i \) in a frequency distribution, or forgetting to divide by \( n \) or \( N \) at the end

topics.name: Mean Deviation about the Median
topics.summary: The mean deviation about the median follows the same idea as the mean deviation about the mean, but measures distances from the median \( M \) instead: \( \text{M.D.}(M) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}|x_i-M| \) for individual data, or \( \text{M.D.}(M) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{n}f_i|x_i-M| \) for frequency data. For individual data, the median is the middle value once the data is arranged in order (or the average of the two middle values, for an even number of observations); for a discrete frequency distribution it is located using cumulative frequencies; for a continuous distribution, the interpolation formula \( M=l+\left(\frac{N/2-cf}{f}\right)h \) is used on the class boundaries. A key theoretical result is that mean deviation is smallest when measured about the median, among all possible reference points  -  smaller even than the mean deviation about the mean. This makes the median a natural 'best' centre for minimising average absolute deviation, even though the mean remains the more commonly used centre for most other statistical purposes.
topics.worked_example: For the data \( 4, 6, 9, 10, 12, 15, 17 \) (\( n=7 \)): arranged in order already, the median is the 4th value, \( M=10 \). Deviations \( x_i-M \): \( -6,-4,-1,0,2,5,7 \). Absolute deviations: \( 6,4,1,0,2,5,7 \), summing to \( 25 \). So \( \text{M.D.}(M)=\dfrac{25}{7}\approx3.5714 \).
common_mistakes: Using the mean instead of the median as the centre (or vice versa) when the question specifically asks for one of the two
Forgetting the absolute value, letting signed deviations from the median cancel instead of adding
For grouped data, locating the median class incorrectly, or forgetting to weight \( |x_i-M| \) by the class frequency \( f_i \)

topics.name: Variance and Standard Deviation — Individual and Discrete Data
topics.summary: Variance measures dispersion using the average of the SQUARED deviations from the mean, rather than absolute deviations: \( \sigma^{2} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\bar{x})^{2} \) for individual data, or \( \sigma^{2} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{n}f_i(x_i-\bar{x})^{2} \) for a discrete frequency distribution. Squaring removes the same cancellation problem that absolute value solves in mean deviation, and also gives larger deviations proportionally more weight. Because squaring changes the units of the data (for example, kg becomes kg\(^2\)), the standard deviation \( \sigma=\sqrt{\sigma^{2}} \) is used to return to the original units, and is the more commonly quoted measure of spread. Two useful properties follow directly from the definition: adding a constant to every observation leaves the variance unchanged (since every deviation from the mean is unchanged), while multiplying every observation by a constant \( k \) multiplies the variance by \( k^{2} \) and the standard deviation by \( |k| \). This chapter covers only individual and discrete data; continuous (grouped) data is handled separately using the shortcut method.
common_mistakes: Taking the absolute value of deviations instead of squaring them (that gives the mean deviation, not the variance)
Reporting the variance when the standard deviation was asked, or vice versa (forgetting to take, or wrongly taking, the square root)
Forgetting to weight by frequency \( f_i \) in a frequency distribution, or dividing by the wrong count instead of \( n \) or \( N \)

topics.name: Variance and Standard Deviation — Continuous Data and the Shortcut Method
topics.summary: For a continuous (grouped) frequency distribution, each class is represented by its mid-point (class mark) \( x_i \), and the variance can in principle be computed directly, just as for discrete data. In practice, especially when class marks are large or awkward numbers, the step-deviation (shortcut) method is used instead: choose a convenient assumed mean \( A \) (usually a middling class mark) and compute \( u_i = \frac{x_i-A}{h} \), where \( h \) is the (common) class width. The variance is then \( \sigma^{2} = h^{2}\left[\frac{1}{N}\sum f_iu_i^{2} - \left(\frac{1}{N}\sum f_iu_i\right)^{2}\right] \), and \( \sigma=\sqrt{\sigma^{2}} \) as before. The final \( h^{2} \) factor restores the units shrunk by dividing by \( h \), and the squared correction term removes any dependence on the particular choice of \( A \)  -  any valid choice gives exactly the same final variance. This method requires all class widths to be equal, since it relies on one shared divisor \( h \) to convert every deviation into a simple, small integer or fraction.
topics.worked_example: For classes \( 0\text{-}10, 10\text{-}20, 20\text{-}30, 30\text{-}40, 40\text{-}50 \) with frequencies \( 5, 8, 15, 16, 6 \) (\( N=50 \)), taking \( A=25 \) and \( h=10 \): \( u_i = -2,-1,0,1,2 \), giving \( \sum f_iu_i=10 \) and \( \sum f_iu_i^{2}=68 \). So \( \sigma^{2}=10^{2}\left[\dfrac{68}{50}-\left(\dfrac{10}{50}\right)^{2}\right]=132 \), and the mean works out to \( \bar{x}=27 \).
common_mistakes: Forgetting to multiply back by \( h^{2} \) at the end, after computing the bracketed step-deviation quantity
Forgetting to subtract the squared correction term \( \left(\frac{1}{N}\sum f_iu_i\right)^{2} \)
Applying the method with unequal class widths, or reporting the variance when the standard deviation (its square root) was asked

topics.name: Analysis of Frequency Distributions — Coefficient of Variation
topics.summary: Standard deviation measures absolute spread, in the same units as the data  -  but this makes it unsafe to directly compare the variability of two data sets that have very different means or are measured in different units. The coefficient of variation solves this by expressing the standard deviation as a percentage of the mean: \( \text{C.V.} = \dfrac{\sigma}{\bar{x}}\times 100 \). Because the units of \( \sigma \) and \( \bar{x} \) cancel in the ratio, C.V. is a pure, unit-independent percentage, making it possible to fairly compare two data sets  -  even ones measured on completely different scales. When comparing two (or more) data sets, the one with the LOWER coefficient of variation is said to be more consistent, or less variable, relative to its own mean; the one with the higher C.V. is more variable. This relative-variability comparison is the main practical use of the coefficient of variation, and is a natural final step once the mean and standard deviation of each distribution are already known.
topics.worked_example: A distribution has mean \( \bar{x}=25 \) and standard deviation \( \sigma=5 \). Then \( \text{C.V.}=\dfrac{5}{25}\times 100=20\% \). If a second distribution has mean \( \bar{x}=40 \) and standard deviation \( \sigma=6 \), its C.V. is \( \dfrac{6}{40}\times 100=15\% \); since \( 15\%<20\% \), the second distribution is relatively more consistent, even though its absolute standard deviation is larger.
common_mistakes: Using the variance \( \sigma^{2} \) instead of the standard deviation \( \sigma \) inside the C.V. ratio
Inverting the ratio (using \( \bar{x}/\sigma \) instead of \( \sigma/\bar{x} \)), or forgetting the \( \times 100 \)
Comparing two data sets' raw standard deviations directly instead of their C.V. values, which is unsafe when their means differ
